name: SonicBench
ability_definition: The ability to detect or tell the differences between sounds that vary in pitch and loudness.

task_realism.reasoning: The psychophysical recognition and comparison tasks on pitch and loudness match how the ability itself is defined and how it is clinically measured. But workplace uses look different: tuning instruments, hearing abnormal machine noises, monitoring alarms or sonar, judging audio quality. Those involve complex, meaningful real-world sounds rather than isolated synthetic tones.

evaluation_conditions.reasoning: Stimuli are clean, controlled, toolbox-generated signals presented one trial at a time, with no background noise, competing sources, time pressure or consequences. Real work often requires picking out faint or subtle differences in noisy, continuous and unpredictable acoustic settings. The direct, tool-free model evaluation is appropriate, but the input distribution is much cleaner than real work.

construct_coverage.reasoning: It covers both components of the ability (pitch and loudness) and both judgment modes (absolute recognition and paired comparison), with human baselines. However, the headline aggregate is diluted by ten other attributes outside this ability, such as spatial, timbre, tempo and counting. It also may not directly probe near-threshold detection of faint sounds, and per-attribute scores are not easily reported.

format_match.reasoning: The input is raw audio, which suits an auditory ability. The outputs are forced-choice or binary judgments on synthetic stimuli, not work artifacts such as a diagnosis of a machine fault, a tuning adjustment or an alert decision. This is a standard psychophysics format rather than a workplace one.

transferability_reasoning: SonicBench is a well-targeted, psychophysically grounded probe of pitch and loudness discrimination that covers both absolute and relative judgments, so it measures the core construct validly. Transfer to workplace capability is moderate: the clean synthetic stimuli, forced-choice outputs and aggregate score diluted by unrelated attributes differ from the noisy, complex, consequence-bearing listening tasks of real work.

2026.metric: overall accuracy (%) averaged across all 12 attributes and both task types; chance is 50%, human average is 91%
2026.human_reference: General adult population with normal hearing, the typical person making everyday pitch and loudness judgments at work. SonicBench's human participants (average 91%) are the proxy.
